Introducing the Saturday Starters Program at Millhaven Swim School
We are pleased to announce a new weekend course for children who are learning to swim for the very first time. Beginning next month, the Saturday Starters Program will offer small-group lessons every Saturday morning for young swimmers between the ages of four and seven. The decision has not been taken lightly. For several terms our weekday beginner sessions have been running at full capacity, and each new intake has left a growing number of households hoping for a place we could not offer. Rather than continue to turn newcomers away, we have chosen to open a second slate of beginner places on Saturdays so that every child who wishes to begin can find one.
Millhaven has served local children for more than fifteen years. The school is led by head coach Rosalind Frayne, who competed at the national level before moving into teaching, and every instructor now on our pool deck was trained personally by Rosalind — including two colleagues she took on this spring — before taking charge of a class of her own.
Households already enrolled with us need do nothing at all. Weekday schedules are unchanged, existing bookings remain valid, and the online account through which you manage them will continue to work as before. The Saturday sessions are reserved strictly for children who are only now beginning to swim; current pupils should therefore stay with their weekday slot rather than transfer across. Merrifield Observatory Opens Its Evenings to the Public
The Halbrook Public Observatory in Merrifield will launch a new after-dark viewing program, Starlight Evenings, beginning on 5 March. Running every week through the spring, the program invites residents to observe the night sky under the guidance of the observatory's staff rather than through a booked private tour.
Central to the program is a newly installed 400-millimeter reflecting telescope, the largest instrument the observatory has ever operated. It is the reason many residents will notice something new about the observatory this spring. Because it requires careful handling and darker conditions, the telescope is dedicated exclusively to the program's advanced deep-sky sessions. The introductory and family sessions will continue to use the observatory's smaller viewing scopes and its outdoor terrace.
"For years our finest equipment was available only to visiting researchers," said Dr. Rosa Meakin, the observatory's director. "This program is about opening those evenings to everyone in Merrifield who has ever wanted to look up and see more of what is there."
The launch comes at a time when chances for public astronomy in the region have grown scarce. The nearby Denholm Science Centre reduced its evening public hours last year following a review of its program spending, and the Ivelford Astronomy Club has since suspended its monthly open sessions, leaving few options for residents hoping to view the sky after dark.
Seats for each session are capped at 20 per evening, and the observatory encourages early booking. A full schedule of the spring sessions appears below.

Protecting the Art You Love: Small Steps That Make a Difference
MARWICK (March 14)—A favorite painting or a framed family photograph can lose its color, and much of its value, faster than most owners expect. Living Spaces Monthly spoke with framing specialist Nadia Sorensen about the simple habits that keep artwork looking its best for decades.
Her first piece of advice concerns location. Never hang a picture where direct sunlight falls on it, she warns, because steady light will fade the colors within a few years. She also recommends keeping artwork out of kitchens and bathrooms, where changing humidity can loosen the paper and encourage mold.
The choice of materials matters just as much. "The single most important decision is the board placed behind the piece," Ms. Sorensen said. "Ordinary cardboard contains acids that turn yellow and stain the artwork, sometimes within months. Only acid-free board will truly protect it." She adds that the glass should be dusted gently and that frames should be kept well away from heaters and radiators.
Readers who would rather leave the work to a professional can visit Halden Framing Studio, which serves the Marwick area from its single location on Pinewood Row. Ms. Sorensen frames every piece with acid-free board, just as she recommends to readers. The studio does not deliver or operate branches in other towns; all framing is completed on site. Studio members are also invited to a free framing workshop held once a month.

Wrenford Gardens Introduces Guided Heritage Walks
WEXBRIDGE (14 February)—Wrenford Botanical Gardens will begin offering a new guided tour, the Wrenford Heritage Garden Walk, on 3 March. Places can be booked from this week.
The gardens were first laid out by Edmund Castellan more than a hundred years ago, when the grounds formed part of a large private estate. For much of the last century the land was closed to the public, and only in recent decades has it become a garden that anyone may visit.
The gardens are now run by their director, Bernard Mott. Visitors can enjoy a carefully restored greenhouse, a plant shop, and the Fernbank Café, all set within the grounds.
Each walk will be led by Margaret Ainsley, the gardens' senior horticulturist, who has cared for the grounds for many years and knows the history of nearly every planting along the route.
Later in the year, the gardens hope to add a series of evening walks for visitors who prefer a quieter time of day.
To reserve a place, visit www.wrenfordgardens.co.uk.
----------------------

Wrenford Heritage Garden Walk — reviewed by Gerald Voss
